source.title: Behavior Beyond Text: Evaluating Refusal Transfer Failure in LLM Agents
source.authors: Ekagra Gupta; R. Saha; Aniekan-Abasi Inyang; Adam Al Gharib

page_placements.theme: Tool-use and agent contexts: chat refusal direction weaker and only partly governs unsafe actions; separate action and injection subspaces

record.tranche_reason: The study applies a harmful-minus-benign difference-in-means direction, ablation, and activation addition to five instruction-tuned models, and measures refusal outcomes, following the original intervention approach on new models.
record.gate_note: The study also evaluates text-to-tool refusal transfer. Those behavioral results are recorded as findings that fit none of the listed versions because the versions do not cover transfer from verbal refusal to tool-call safety. The study reports direction-selection details, but those values were used to select the layer and are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: It applies the original harmful-minus-benign difference-in-means direction, all-layer directional ablation, 1× activation addition and the KL admissibility check to five new instruct models. It judges refusal on no-tool harmful and benign prompts (Tables 3, 6, 7) and states that the original result reproduces only in part. The tool-call analyses (patching, suppression, AUC, steering) measure tool-call safety, a different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that the authors state the Arditi et al. single-direction result reproduces only in part in text. Ablation lowers refusal in Command-R, Mistral and Llama but raises it in Qwen and Gemma, and addition works only in Qwen and Llama. The direction is a strong predictor but only a partial mediator and blunt control of tool-call safety.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful-minus-benign difference-in-means directions and causal ablation/addition across five instruction-tuned models. It selects layers within a 35–85% depth band, includes tool-context activation patching and KL checks, and tests transfer to tool-call behavior. It does not use a weight edit.
record.method_sensitivity: Direction ablation/addition effects differ substantially by model. Tool-context activation suppression is absent for Llama but reported for four other models. System-prompt framing changes conditioned divergence; adversarial stress also changes it by model. The paper reports strong steering costs and flags conditions with at least 25% degenerate outputs as uninterpretable.

fits_no_version.finding: Harmful requests refused in no-tool chat still yield unsafe tool calls (conditioned divergence 0.10–0.52 normal, 0.10–0.66 stress). The gap is modulated but not closed by system prompts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Verbal refusal does not reliably transfer to tool-call safety in instruction-tuned models.

fits_no_version.finding: The refusal direction's activation drops in tool contexts in four of five models and predicts unsafe calls (AUC 0.76–0.86). Restoring it reverts only 13–90% of unsafe calls, mostly by suppressing the call, and 80–96% of remaining calls stay unsafe.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The text refusal direction partially mediates whether a model acts with tools, not how safely it acts.

record.problems: The KL check is not a broad capability evaluation, and only Command-R passes the selected-layer admissibility check. Some intervention conditions have substantial degenerate output. Patching often suppresses tool calls instead of converting unsafe calls to safe ones. The action environment scores generated calls with deterministic predicates and does not execute them; the authors note that tool availability and tool-oriented wording vary jointly.
record.rows_left_out: At the 60-row cap, omitted the detailed steering coefficient grid (Table 9), ablation controls and ablation-on-tool-call outcomes (Tables 6 and 8), and full text refusal rates and tool-use rates (Table 1). The steering grid includes substantial collateral reductions in benign tool use and degenerate-output conditions; the authors summarize these in Sections 5–7. Direction-selection layer values were excluded as selection-only results.

untested.parts: No broad capability benchmarks beyond the next-token KL check; no weight edit.
No test that jailbreaks suppress the direction, and no adversarial training against ablation. Stress mode is only measured behaviourally.
No comparison of single versus affine, cone or multi-direction representations. Extra directions are only offered as a possible explanation.
Only a cosine between harm-contrast and refused-vs-complied directions at one token. No separate decoding of harmfulness versus refusal across positions.
Directions are extracted per model. The text-vs-tool context cosine is not a language, variant or base-to-instruct transfer.
No comparison of training methods or stages.
Run in no-think mode; no reasoning-model test.

missing.what: Activation addition at higher multiples: Qwen 1.5× 0.53 (18% degenerate), Mistral 2× 0.06, Llama 2× 0.34. Most other cells are degenerate. Bears on whether stronger addition induces refusal.
Dataset-prompt KL column (2.31, 0.91, 0.14, 10.95, 0.40) and count of passing layers per model (e.g. 0/17 Mistral, 0/32 Gemma)

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 links were removed. Patching, suppression and AUC concern tool-call safety and do not compare representation geometries. The random-direction ablation control (Table 6: refusal unchanged, e.g. 0.78→0.78 Qwen) is declared in rows_left_out but would support specificity of the effects. Steering costs (Table 9) and ablation on tool calls (Table 8) belong with the tool-call fits_no_version finding. The selected layers sit at 81–84% depth, near the top of the search band, which may contribute to the weak replication.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports KL checks and selected tool-use costs, but does not establish that broad general capabilities remain intact. It tests activation ablation/addition, not a weight edit.
No test that attacks suppress the direction, or that training against its ablation improves robustness.

The study does not directly compare affine, cone, or multi-direction representations. Its partial-mediation results concern tool-call safety, and additional directions are suggested as a possible explanation.
It compares harmful-versus-benign and refused-versus-complied directions, but does not independently decode a harmfulness judgment and a refusal decision.
Directions are extracted separately for each model; no cross-language, base-to-instruct, or shared-direction transfer test.
No comparison of refusal-training methods, data, or training stages.
No reasoning-model comparison; the appendix describes the transcripts as no-think.

labels.reason: Refusal rose 78→94% and 66→100%, while random-direction ablation left it at 0.78 and 0.68 (Table 6). Gemma's result is for the mean-out variant only.

labels.label: challenges
labels.condition: 1× activation addition in Mistral-7B and Gemma-3-27B
labels.reason: Benign refusal stays 0.00 and 0.01 at 1×. Mistral reaches only 0.06 at 2×, and Gemma degenerates above 1×.

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.condition: Ablation in Mistral-7B, Command-R-7B and Llama-3.1-70B
labels.reason: Refusal falls but 33–59% remains (R27, R28, R30). The authors call Llama's drop small.

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.condition: 1× activation addition in Qwen3-14B and Llama-3.1-70B
labels.reason: Induction is partial: 0.33 and 0.24 at 1× (R31, R35).

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.condition: Ability-preservation KL check in Qwen3-14B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-3-27B and Llama-3.1-70B
labels.reason: Generic-prompt KL of 0.25–11.34 exceeds the <0.1 criterion. That is a cost the version says shouldn't occur.

labels.label: supports
labels.reason: R28 (68→33%) is partial and already sits in the limits_scope group. Dataset-prompt KL 0.14 fails and 1× addition is 50% degenerate. supports fits only a KL-only condition (R38, generic prompts).

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.condition: All five models, decision token at the selected layer
labels.reason: Cosine 0.69–0.86 at a single token, which the authors read as largely shared. This is a robustness check, not a cross-position test, so limits_scope fits better than challenges.

relation.reason: Reports its own ablation, addition and KL results on five models and says Arditi et al. reproduces only in part.

tranche.reason: Uses harmful-minus-benign diff-in-means at the decision token, all-layer ablation, 1× addition and Arditi's KL check, scored by refusal rate. Deviations: layer picked by max norm in a 35–85% band, not refusal/KL validation; Claude Opus 5 judge.

source_check.notes: The layer is picked by largest diff-in-means norm and lands at 81–84% depth; at that layer only Command-R's direction passes KL, so some V1 failures may come from layer choice rather than the claim. Tables 6–7 end with an unplaced 'n=120' footnote, probably for Llama-3.1-70B, which may explain why Table 3 gives 71→59% and Table 6 gives 0.69→0.62.

statements.correction: Absent at 1×: Mistral-7B 0.00, Gemma-3-27B 0.01. Partial at 1×: Qwen3-14B 0.33, Llama-3.1-70B 0.24 (0× baseline 0.01). Qwen reaches 0.53 at 1.5× (18% degenerate); Llama reaches 0.34 at 2× (8% degenerate).
statements.problem: Under a 'little or no refusal' challenges entry, but this study's Qwen 0.33 and Llama 0.24 are partial induction and labelled limits_scope in its own verdicts.

statements.correction: All values are generic-prompt KLs (48 ordinary requests). Dataset benign-prompt KLs are 2.31, 0.91, 0.14 (Command-R), 10.95 and 0.40.
Only the 66%→100% ablation uses mean-out. KL 11.34 is for raw r̂text all-layer ablation, whose refusal outputs were ≥25% degenerate (Table 6 ‡). The 1× addition (0.01) uses the diff-in-means gap.
statements.problem: 'Uses a mean-out variant for Gemma' reads as covering all three numbers, but it applies only to the ablation refusal rate.

statements.correction: KL 0.04 is on generic prompts. On the benchmark's benign prompts Command-R's KL is 0.14.

statements.problem: The shown text is truncated and names no result from this study, so it can't be checked.
The shown text is truncated and names no result from this study, so it can't be checked.

statements.correction: Capability evidence is next-token KL on 48 generic and on benchmark benign prompts, plus degenerate-output screening. No capability benchmark. All other numbers match Tables 3, 5, 6 and 7.
statements.problem: 'capability y' overstates it: the only ability check is next-token KL, which the record's own verdict fix calls an admissibility check, not a capability benchmark.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Mistral-7B, Command-R-7B, and Llama-3.1-70B ablation; Qwen3-14B and Llama-3.1-70B addition
reader_labels.reason: Ablation lowered refusal only incompletely for Mistral, Command-R, and Llama; addition produced partial benign over-refusal for Qwen and Llama. See R27, R28, R30, R31, R35.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Qwen3-14B and Gemma-3-27B ablation; Mistral-7B and Gemma-3-27B addition
reader_labels.reason: Ablation increased rather than reduced harmful-prompt refusal in Qwen and Gemma; addition had no effect at 1× in Mistral or Gemma. See R26, R29, R32, R34.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: All five models on the generic-request KL check
reader_labels.reason: Only Command-R's reported generic KL value is below the stated <0.1 criterion; the others exceed it, limiting the claim that abilities remain intact. This is a KL check, not a broad capability benchmark. See R36–R40.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Tool-enabled harmful prompts across the five models
reader_labels.reason: Patching the one projection reverted only a share of unsafe calls in four models, and most reversions were no-call rather than safe-call outcomes; this supports treating the direction as an incomplete account/control of tool-call safety. See R41–R45.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: All five models at their selected operating layers
reader_labels.reason: The harmful-versus-benign and refusal-versus-compliance directions had cosine similarities of 0.693–0.859, which the authors describe as largely sharing a direction rather than being separately encoded. See R46–R50.
